newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi army says it killed 140 Hutu rebels.
newsitem.headline: Burundi army says it killed 140 Hutu rebels.

text.p: Burundi's army said on Monday troops killed 140 Hutu rebels in battles last week in the south of the country.

An army statement said three soldiers were killed and eight wounded in fighting in Mabanda commune near the Tanzanian border. Forty rebels, operating from mountains stretching from Mabanda to Nyanza Lac, were killed in Mabanda, and 100 were killed in Rukamizasi, north of Nyanza Lac. It made no mention of civilian casualties.
There was no independent confirmation of the army report.

More than 150,000 people, mostly civilians, have been killed in massacres and civil war between Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army and rebels from the majority Hutu tribe since troops killed Burundi's Hutu president in 1993.

In the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha, Burundi's Foreign Minister Luc Rukingama said he hoped a regional summit opening there on Wednesday would lift sanctions imposed on the Central African nation last year.
"There is no ground to maintain sanctions and it is good for the neighbouring countries to come out with a positive solution," he told a news conference.
Regional leaders imposed sanctions on Burundi after Major Pierre Buyoya, a Tutsi, overthrew Burundi's civilian government headed by Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya last July.

But the trade and transport sanctions, designed to force Buyoya to negotiate with the Hutu rebels, have largely failed to work because of Zaire's civil war which opened up new trade routes in rebel-held territory and smuggling.

Uganda, Tanzania, Kenya, Zambia, Rwanda and officials from the Organisation of African Unity and the United Nations are scheduled to attend the one-day summit to be preceded by talks of foreign ministers. Buyoya has also been invited.

"We wish that the summit will respond to the needs of the population which are the majority and the ones feeling the pinch of the sanctions, especially children, the elderly and the sick," Rukingama said.

In a separate incident in Bujumbura, witnesses said a soldier on Sunday killed two policemen in the centre of the city and a gendarme was killed in crossfire. They had no explanation for the soldier opening fire.
Military authorities refused to comment on the incident.
A defence ministry official, who declined to be identified, described it as "unfortunate" but said it was of no immediate importance since the army was fighting rebels in the south.

State radio meanwhile quoted returned Burundian refugees as saying camps in Tanzania were training bases for Hutu rebels fighting to topple military ruler Pierre Buyoya, a Tutsi who seized power last July.

It said rebels of the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD) were mostly former refugees who had fled to camps in Tanzania from eastern Zaire late last year. The CNDD is Burundi's largest rebel group and is led by Leonard Nyangoma.
